A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_

Chitosan Polysaccharides Activated carbon

CaO and Al2O3 nanoparticles Olive stones-biochar Adsorption

A B S T R A C T

The present work concerns the preparation of hydrogel composite beads based on activated carbon@metal oxide (M: CaO, Al2O3, CaO/Al2O3) from the calcination of olive stones biomass encapsulated by chitosan as a cross-linking matrix. The biocomposites were characterized by SEM, BET, Zeta potential, TGA, XRD and FTIR in order to investigate the morphological, thermal, textural and structural properties of these solids. The encap-sulation of activated carbon-based nanocomposites leaded to obtain a porous structure. The nanocomposite beads were used as biosorbents for the MB and OG dyes removal. Several parameters affecting the adsorption process were investigated such as effect of the pH, dyes concentration, temperature and time. The adsorption

process follows the Langmuir isotherm with R2 ≈ 1 and the pseudo-second order model confirming the uniform,

monolayer, endothermic and chemisorption nature of the dye’s adsorption. All biosorbents showed a higher affinity to anionic dye “Orange G (OG)” due to their positive surface charge. The CSAC@Ca showed the best adsorption capacity Qmax = 323.625 mg/g against OG while the CSAC@Al showed the best adsorption capacity

Qmax = 134.589 mg/g against methylene blue. Finally, the hydrogel beads were reused in five successive cycles

and showed very good efficiency even at the last cycle contrary to the parent chitosan.

# Introduction

Our planet has been facing Global water crises in the last decades and this shortage of water is projected to worsen by a very big margin in the coming decades. Water quality is the ultimate challenge facing hu-manity due to the increasing water pollution caused by industrial development and the discharge of organic and inorganic pollutants \[[1](#_bookmark32),[2](#_bookmark33)\]. Among these contaminants, organic dyes from textile and

pharmaceutical industries are one of the most common especially the methylene blue (MB) and orange G (OG) \[[3](#_bookmark34)\]. Evey year, more than 70 million tons of synthetic dyes are produced but more than 280.000 tons are discharged into wastewater in the nature due to several factor such as fail during textile dyeing procedures \[[4](#_bookmark35)\]. The problem with these molecules is that they are non-biodegradable due to their synthetic and very stable structures which make them very toxic to the environment and all living species \[[5](#_bookmark36)\]. In marine systems these dyes minimize light

penetration which lead to the increasing of Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) conducing to the inhibition of aquatic vegetation and perturba-tion of the food chain of marine species \[[4](#_bookmark35),[6](#_bookmark37)\]. For human, the dyes toxicity led to several problem such as the reproductive system, renal functions, hepatocytes, and the central nervous system in addition to various cancer \[[4](#_bookmark35),[7](#_bookmark38),[8](#_bookmark39)\]. For these reasons, their elimination become a serious priority and several techniques such as coagulation and floccu-lation, AOP, biological treatment, photocatalysis and adsorption have emerged to purify the water \[[9–13](#_bookmark40)\]. Among these techniques, adsorp-tion is one of the most popular technique due to its high efficiency, rapidity, low cost and environmentally friendly nature since no toxins are produced during or after the process \[[14–18](#_bookmark42)\]. However, the choice of a good adsorbent is important to optimize the adsorption process in term of time, results and cost, therefore adsorbents like polymers, zeo-lites, clays, mesoporous materials and metal oxide are frequently used \[[19](#_bookmark43),[20](#_bookmark44)\].

Activated carbon from biomass are one of the most studied adsor-bents during the last decades \[[21](#_bookmark45),[22](#_bookmark46)\]. These porous materials have attracted the attention of several researcher groups due to their high efficiency in the adsorption of several contaminants including organic and inorganic ones, their high surface area, their porosity, their low toxicity, their very low cost and many active sites for adsorption \[[23–25](#_bookmark47)\]. Furthermore, the adsorption capacity of the activated carbon can be more impressive by dispersing metal oxide nanoparticles such as the magnetite Fe3O4, calcium oxide (CaO), Aluminum oxide Al2O3…and more \[[26–28](#_bookmark48)\]. Indeed, it has been proven that the CaO and Al2O3 in-crease the surface area, provide more functional groups for electrostatic interactions, adjust the surface pH which led to a better affinity with some pollutants, and improve the thermal stability of the resulting nanocomposite which improve the efficiency of the material for removing dyes from aqueous solutions \[[29](#_bookmark49),[30](#_bookmark50)\]. However, despite these several advantages, the activated carbon or its nanocomposite are generally used as very fine particles during the adsorption which highly complicate their recovering and their reuse, requiring techniques such as ultrafiltration and centrifugation to separate them from the solution. To overcome these problems, the encapsulation of fine particles in polysaccharides matrix to make beads or membranes is one the best option that make possible to facilitate their separation, reduce the toxicity, controlled size, easy reuse and effectiveness in various fields such as biological and environmental \[[31–35](#_bookmark51)\]. Carbohydrate polymers like polysaccharides can also protect the coated material from degra-dation and prevent the particle aggregation and the leaching \[[10](#_bookmark41),[36–39](#_bookmark52)\]. Chitosan is a linear cationic polysaccharide known to be biodegradable, low cost, ecofriendly and easy to encapsulate different materials \[[19](#_bookmark43),[40](#_bookmark53)\]. Indeed, contrary to the majority of natural poly-saccharides (which are usually neutral or anionic), chitosan has a pos-itive surface charge. This makes it interactive with negatively charged molecules, cells, and surfaces. Chitosan is rich of hydroxyl (OH) and amine (NH2) functional groups, the abundance of these groups facili-tates chemical modifications, improving solubility, encapsulation effi-ciency and increases the amount and variety of active sites available in the obtained nanocomposite for binding dye molecules or heavy metals \[[41–43](#_bookmark54)\]. Moreover, Chitosan increases the hydrophilic nature of the materials facilitating water absorption and enhances the dispersion of the adsorbent in the solutions which allows a better interaction between the adsorbent and pollutants dissolved in water, leading to greater adsorption capacity \[[44](#_bookmark55),[45](#_bookmark56)\]. In addition to that, chitosan has a pH-responsive behaviour which means that the protonation/deprotona-tion of amino groups allows selective adsorption, making it adaptable

for different environmental conditions \[[46](#_bookmark57)\].

The main objective of this work is the preparation of novel adsorbent beads composed of olive stone-derived activated carbon, Al2O3/CaO, and chitosan for the efficient removal of both cationic (methylene blue, MB) and anionic (orange G, OG) dyes from aqueous solutions. The presence of activated carbon provides a high surface area for adsorption while the incorporation of metal oxides (Al2O3 and CaO) is expected to

introduce additional functional sites, enhance surface charge properties, and improve dye affinity. The presence of both Al2O3 and CaO allows simultaneous adsorption of oppositely charged dyes by exploiting elec-trostatic interactions, ion exchange, and surface complexation mecha-nisms. A comparative study between chitosan beads and their metal-oxide-based nanocomposites was conducted to elucidate the role of polysaccharide encapsulation in enhancing adsorption performance, improving material stability, and facilitating reusability. The adsorption process was systematically studied by evaluating the effects of contact time, initial dye concentration, pH, and temperature for all materials, along with their reusability potential. Furthermore, the structural, thermal, and morphological properties of these adsorbents were ana-lysed in-depth to correlate their physicochemical characteristics with adsorption behaviour.

# Materials and methods

- 1.  _Materials_

Chitosan powder (high molecular weight, CAS Number: 9012-76-4, 310,000–375,000 Da, >75 % deacetylated), Calcium chloride (CaCl2, CAS Number: 10043–52-4, MW: 110.98 g/mol), Aluminum nitrate

nonahydrate (Al(NO3)3.9H2O, CAS Number: 7784-27-2, MW: 375.13 g/ mol), Methylene blue (MB, CAS Number: 122965–43-9, MW: 319.85 g.

mol—1, ≥97.0 %), Orange G (OG, CAS Number: 1936-15-8, MW: 452.37 g.mol—1), n-Hexane (CH3(CH2)4CH3, CAS Number: 110–54-3, MW:

86.18 g.mol—1, ≥95 %), Acetic acid (CH3CO2H, CAS Number: 64–19-7, MW: 60.05 g/mol), Sodium hydroxide reagent grade ≥ 98 % (NaOH,

CAS Number: 1310-73-2, MW: 40.00 g/mol) were all purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. The pollutant solutions used in this study were prepared using deionised water with a pH = 6.5 and a conductivity = 1.3 μs. The

olive used in study collected from the region of Tlemcen on the north-

west coast of Algeria.

The functional groups for all materials have been studied using FTIR BRUKER ALPHA Platinum-ATR in the interval 4000–400 cm—1, the structural proprieties of the obtained nancomposites were confirmed by

X-ray diffraction (XRD) using Bruker D8 A25 Powder diffractometer (Cu-Kα-radiation). The morphology of the hydrogel’s beads was deter-mined by SEM on the HITASHI SU8010 microscope. The thermal properties of the materials were analysed by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) using Netzsch STA 449 F3 Jupiter under a nitrogen flow in the

temperature range 30–800 ◦C. The surface charge of the biosorbents was

followed by Zeta potential using the Malvern-Zetasizer Nano S90. The ultrasonicator used during this study is a Branson digital 450 ultrasound generator.

- 1.  _Preparation of chitosan beads_

The chitosan beads were prepared as follows: 2 g of chitosan were dissolved in a mixture of 98 mL of deionised water and 2 mL of acetic acid. The mixture was stirred for 6 h until total homogenisation and disappearance of bubbles. The chitosan beads were obtained by dripped the mixture using a syringe in a sodium hydroxide solution to get a solid beads form. The beads were leaved in this solution of (NaOH, 2 M, 250 mL) for 24 h. The solid were then filtered, washed and stored in deionised water to maintain their hydrogel state. The chitosan beads were named “CST”.

- 1.  _Preparation of activated carbon@metal oxide (CaO and Al2O3)_

Activated carbon were prepared from olive stones as vegetable, biocompatible and green source. Firstly, olive stones were collected and washed well then dried a 90 ◦C overnight. The stones were then crushed

in order to get a medium-fine particle size. The powder was immersed in

hexane for 24 h to remove any oily residues from the inside or outside the olive stone. Once done, the powder was washed, dried and stocked

for the next step of preparation \[[26](#_bookmark48)\]. Then, 3 masses of obtained biomass (10 g each) was mixed with 3 different metallic solution, the first contain CaCl2 (0.1 M, 100 mL), the second contain Al(NO3)3 (0.1 M, 100 mL) and the third as a mixture between both of metallic solution (50 mL of each solution). The three mixtures were sonicated for 30 min in an amplitude of 50 % then stirred for 3 h. The use of ultrasound treatment facilitates uniform dispersion of metal cations within the biomass pore network. The acoustic cavitation and acoustic streaming lead to for-mation and collapsing of microbubbles in the mixture producing an extremely localized heat and violent fluid flow generating a high energy in the reaction medium \[[9](#_bookmark40),[47](#_bookmark58)\]. This energy allows to disrupts particle agglomeration and promotes cation diffusion into the carbon matrix. The magnetic stirring allows then the slow dispersion and stabilization of large metal cation amount in the active site of the biomass. All mix-tures were filtered and dried under vacuum. The obtained powders were

calcinated at 700 ◦C at a heating rate of 5 ◦C/min to mitigate structural

collapse and preserve the hierarchical porosity. This thermal treatment accomplishes two critical functions: pyrolyzing the olive stone biomass to yield a porous activated carbon framework and inducing the thermal decomposition of the precursor salts, CaCl2 and Al(NO3)3, into their respective metal oxides (CaO and Al2O3). Finally, the obtained carbons

were then washed by HCl solution (0.1 M, pH = 1) to remove any im-

purities and then washed several times with deionised water to neutralise the acidic pH. Finally, the resulting activated carbon-metal oxide were dried at 50 ◦C overnight. The prepared samples were

named respectively (AC@CaO, AC@Al2O3 and AC@CaO/Al2O3).

- 1.  _Preparation of chitosan@activated carbon-metal oxide_

Firstly, three masses of chitosan (2 g) were dissolved in 2 % acetic acid-water solutions. The mixtures were stirred until homogenisation and a bubble-free solution was obtained. Then 1.1 g of each activated carbon nanocomposite was added to the previous chitosan solutions and stirred at room temperature. The mixtures were dripped using a syringe to aqueous sodium hydroxide solutions. The obtained beads were left in a (2 M, 250 mL) solution of NaOH for 24 h. Finally, the beads were filtered, washed and preserved in deionised water to maintain their hydrogel state ([Scheme 1](#_bookmark10)). The obtained nanocomposites beads were named CSAC@CA, CSAC@AL and CSAC@ALCA.

- 1.  _Adsorption experiments_

The organic dyes adsorption in the simple system was studied as following: firstly, a stock solution of methylene blue (MB) and orange G (OG) at 1200 ppm were prepared by dissolving the dyes powder in deionised water. Then, several concentrations of 4, 150, 400, and 800 ppm for each dye were obtained by diluting the stock solution with deionised water. All adsorption experiments were conducted by mixing 10 mL of dyes solution with 2 beads of biosorbents hydrogel (around 10 mg) using a wrist action shaker at room temperature. Once done, the materials were separated from the solution and the residual dye solu-tions were determined by U_V_–Visible spectroscopy at wavelength 680 and 470 nm for MB and OG, respectively. All experiments were repeated three time leading to average values. The organic dyes adsorbed amount (Qt) and removal efficiency (%) were calculated using Eq. [(1)](#_bookmark11) and Eq. [(2)](#_bookmark12), respectively.

For this study, two models were studied: pseudo-first order and pseudo-second order.

Among the different operational experimental factors that affect the adsorption process, pH is considered as one of the most crucial param-eters. The experiments were performed at various pH values ranging from 2 to 10. The pH was adjusted to the desired value by adding HCl (0.1 M) or NaOH (0.1 M) and was recorded using a pH meter. Both of MB and OG adsorption experiments were carried out using an adsorbent dosage, initial concentration and solution temperature of 10:10 (mg/

mL), 150 ppm and 28 ◦C respectively. The adsorption efficiency is

measured by analysing the supernatants by UV–Visible spectroscopy \[[2](#_bookmark33),[40](#_bookmark53)\].

The adsorption isotherms were studied in order to understand and describe the relation between the amount of the organic dyes adsorbed and the adsorbent which help to characterize the adsorption behaviour, to determinate the maximal adsorption capacity of the prepared mate-rials and even to explain some interaction between the species. For this purpose, the following mathematical models are widely used to translate the experimental results: Langmuir isotherm, which supposes a homo-geneous monolayer adsorption is expressed by Eq. overlapped band of C — H stretching at 2800–3000 cm—1 \[[50](#_bookmark60),[51](#_bookmark61)\], the C–O stretching vibration of the amide groups at 1650 cm—1. The band at 1656 cm—1 is attributed to the stretching vibrations of N — H amide groups of chitosan. The bending vibration of N — H amine groups that appears normally around 1590 cm—1 show a shift to low wavenumber until 1520 cm—1, this shifting is mainly due to the crosslinking as hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions between chitosan and

metal oxides \[[52](#_bookmark62)\]. The C — H bending of the polysaccharide is observed at 1377 cm—1 and the stretching vibration of the C — O band belonging to the chitosan backbone is localized at 1020–1090 cm—1 \[[53](#_bookmark63),[54](#_bookmark64)\]. The several characteristic bands of the activated carbon are also visible and a broad band in the region of 3500–3100 cm—1 attributed to the vibration of the O — H band and overlapped with the N — H band, confirming the hydrophilic nature of the chitosan, activated carbon and the metal oxide, the symmetric and asymmetric stretching vibration of C — H bond of the AC is also overlapped in this zone \[[26](#_bookmark48)\]. The stretching vibration of the C–C band appears approximately around 1540 cm—1. The metal oxide specific bands appears generally in the region >900 cm—1 \[[55](#_bookmark65),[56](#_bookmark66)\]. The Ca—O present two band of stretching vibration at 550 cm—1 and 877

cm—1 confirming the presence of CaO nanoparticles \[[57](#_bookmark67)\]. In case of Al2O3, the specific stretching bands of Al—O group are observed at 560 cm—1 and in the region between 700 and 950 cm—1 \[[58](#_bookmark68),[59](#_bookmark69)\]. Another characteristic band are noticed at 1355 cm—1 which is attributed to the

Al–O bond \[[60](#_bookmark70)\]. Finally, all these bands are broader and more intense in the case of the CSAC@ALCA which is due to the fact that this nano-composite contain both CaO and Al2O3.

- -   1.  _X_–_ray diffraction pattern_

The XRD patterns of chitosan-based nanocomposites were exposed in [Fig. 1](#_bookmark18)(b). The spectra show the presence of the chitosan, activated car-bon and the metal oxide nanoparticles which are more intense. The peaks localized around 2θ = 9.10◦ and 20.23◦ are attributed respectively

to the (020) and (110) network plans of the chitosan beads, two other

weak peaks can also be observed around 24◦ and 43◦ corresponding respectively to (002) and (100) crystallographic planes of the activated carbon. For the calcium oxide-based beads, the peaks at 2θ = 32.28◦, 37.45◦, 54◦, 64.33◦, 67.56◦, 79.89◦ and 88.79◦ corresponding to the

(111), (200), (220), (311), (222), (400) and (331) networks planes of CaO according to the JCPDS card no. 75-0264 \[[61](#_bookmark71)\]. These peaks confirm the structure of the CaO dispersed in the organic matrix but show also

the presence of a Ca(OH)2 phase at 20.73◦, 47.28◦, 51.88◦ and 64.19◦ attributed to the (011), (012), (110) and (021) crystallographic planes \[[62](#_bookmark72)\]. The presence of the Ca(OH)2 phase is due to two factor, the first is

the contact with water inside the beads favorize the formation of this molecule and the second factor is the calcination temperature (700 ◦C) used for the preparation of the activated carbon@CaO. Indeed, V. E.

Gonzaga et al., in their precious work confirmed that a calcination temperature of 900 ◦C is needed to obtain a pure phase of CaO nano-particles \[[63](#_bookmark73)\]. For the CSAC@Al containing the Al2O3, the peaks

observed at 2θ = 25.58◦, 35.13◦, 37.78◦, 43.36◦, 52.54◦, 57.51◦, 61.16◦, 61.34◦, 66.54◦, 68.19◦, 76.88◦, 77.23◦, 80.69◦, 84.37◦, 86.36◦ and

89.01◦ are attributed to the (012), (104), (110), (113), (024), (116),

(211), (122), (018), (214), (300), (1010), (119), (220), (223), (312) and

(0210) plans of the aluminum oxide nanoparticles according to the JCPDS card no. 10-0173 \[[64](#_bookmark74)\]. Finally, the CSAC@ALCA containing a mixture of both metal oxides have shown both network plans of both nanoparticles confirming their presence but with some shifting observed in addition to some amorphous phases. The shifting in the case of the mixture is related to several parameters such as the lattice stress, intercalation of atoms into the crystal lattice, phase transitions and the difference between the size of each oxide alone and in the mixture.

The XRD analysis not only confirms the crystalline nature of the adsorbent but also allows estimation of the crystallite size using the Debye-Scherrer equation (Eq. [(13)](#_bookmark19)), which can be very helpful for the adsorption study since a small particle size is usually related to better activity \[[2](#_bookmark33)\]. For this reason, the average crystallite size of the metal oxide nanoparticles contained in each adsorbent was determined using the Eq. [(13)](#_bookmark19):

_D_ \= _K_._λ_/_β_.cos_θ_ (13)

where D is the crystallite size (nm), K is the shape factor (0.9), λ is the X-ray wavelength (0.15406 nm for Cu-Kα radiation), β is the full width at half maximum (FWHM) after instrumental broadening correction, and θ is the Bragg diffraction angle \[[65](#_bookmark75)\]. The calculations were performed using the most intense diffraction peak for each phase to ensure reliable crystallite size estimation. The analysis revealed that the crystallite sizes of CaO averaged 23.19 nm which can be considered as very small size compared to those found in the literature from conventional methods \[[66](#_bookmark76),[67](#_bookmark77)\]. In case of Al2O3 from the CSAC@Al, the obtained particle size were 37.94 nm are well within the typical small sizes observed from previous studies \[[68](#_bookmark78)\]. These small particles size observed is mainly due to the ultrasonic treatment as dispersion methods, sonication process provide an efficient breakdown of agglomerates and enhanced nucle-ation control. Ultrasonic cavitation generates localized high-energy in the reaction medium, inducing rapid mixing and uniform distribution of metal cations within the matrix \[[9](#_bookmark40),[47](#_bookmark58)\]. Moreover, this treatment mini-mizes particle coalescence and promotes homogeneous precipitation upon subsequent oxidation or thermal treatment. Additionally, the sonication-assisted dispersion enhances interaction between the matrix and metal species, restricting uncontrolled growth and favoring the formation of ultrafine metal oxide particles with improved surface area and reactivity \[[9](#_bookmark40),[47](#_bookmark58)\]. For CSAC@ALCA containing a mixed oxide (CaO/ Al2O3), a crystallite size of 20.54 nm was observed which is smaller than both metal oxide size individually. This phenomenon is due to several reason such as the inhibition of crystallite growth since the metal oxide together may form complex phases instead of existing as individual oxides which disrupt the growth of pure metal oxide crystallites in addition to the lattice strain and defects generated by the presence of

multiple cations (Ca2+ and Al3+). The different crystallization behaviour is also an important reason since pure CaO and Al2O3 crystallize more

easily into larger crystallites due to their simpler structures while in mixed system, the competition between Ca2+ and Al3+ for incorporation into the lattice can slow down crystallization kinetics, resulting in

smaller crystallites. One more cause can justify this smaller size is that mixed oxide system may contain fraction of amorphous or poorly

crystalline phases that do not contribute to XRD peak broadening, making the detectable crystallites appear smaller. In contrast, pure CaO and Al2O3 show higher crystallinity leading to larger apparent crystallite sizes.

- -   1.  _Zeta potential_

Zeta potential is an important analysis that allow to explain the af-finities between the adsorbent and the organic dyes and the adsorption mechanism, that’s why the analysis was carried out at a pH region from 3 to 11 and represented in [Fig. 1](#_bookmark18)(c). The figure show that all biosorbents show a positive surface although the pH range which confirm the

encapsulation by the chitosan, a biopolymer very known for its positive surface charge \[[53](#_bookmark63)\]. Below pH = 5, the surface charge is very high due to the high concentration of the H+ proton in the solution at this pH range which provoke the ionization of amine groups on the chitosan surface to

get the C–NH3+ groups.

Beyond this pH, the surface charge decreases progressively due to the increasing of the hydroxyl ions concentration (OH—) leading to the deprotonation of the amine groups of the chitosan matrix and the (OH)

groups available on the surface of chitosan, activated carbon and even metal oxide. The CSAC@Al showed a higher zeta potential than the CSAC@Ca which is due to the fact that Al2O3 is well known to have a lower isoelectric point (IEP) than the CaO which led to an easier deprotonation, for these reasons the combination of both metal oxide showed a more positive surface than the Al2O3\-based nanocomposite but less positive than the calcium oxide adsorbent.

- -   1.  _Thermogravimetric analysis_

The thermogravimetric analysis of the three chitosan-based nano-composites beads was presented in the [Fig. 1](#_bookmark18)(d). Before the analysis, the beads were dried at 45 ◦C for 24 h to minimize the presence of water as

much as possible. The composite beads showed three mass losses. The

first loss located in the range of 50–200 ◦C due to the evaporation of the physisobed water and the breaking of the bonds between the water and –OH, –NH2 and –COOH groups of chitosan and activated carbon \[[69](#_bookmark79)\].

The second mass loss in the range of 200–550 ◦C attributed to the ma-

terials degradation, this second weight loss can be characterized by two stages, the first between 200 and 300 ◦C including the depolymerization of the biopolymer and the breaking of glycosidic bonds which generate

the acetic acid, formaldehyde and various volatile organic compounds in addition to the ammonia (NH3) release after the deacetylation of chi-tosan. The second stage from 300 to 550 ◦C characterized by the

decomposition of the pyranose ring of the chitosan and the several

oxygen-based functional groups such as the carboxylic acid, phenolic groups, carbonyl, etc. of the activated carbon which generate the CO2, CO, CH4, NH3 and other carbonaceous material. Finally, the third mass loss above 550 ◦C corresponding to the oxidative degradation of the

carbonaceous residue remaining from the previous mass loss step into

gaseous products and the dihydroxylation of the Ca(OH)2 groups observed in from XRD analysis.

- -   1.  _Scanning electron microscopy (SEM)_

The morphology of the CSAC@Ca, CSAC@Al and CSAC@ALCA hydrogels beads were observed by scanning electron microscopy and the obtained images were regrouped in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark20). The outside surface of nanocomposites beads shows a clear roughness, irregular and shriveled due to the presence of activated carbon@metal oxide and these obser-vations are very frequent in the chitosan-based beads. However, the CSAC@ALCA hydrogel composite have a rougher surface then other beads with apparent stains of the Aluminum/Calcium-oxide complex, the stains are very well dispersed over all the surface. The SEM images inside these hydrogels show the presence of metal oxide crystal and a porous structure especially in the case of the CSAC@ALCA. In the case of the calcium oxide-based composite, the porosity is more like splits than cavities. These larges and various pores are mainly due to the presence of the activated which is well known as a highly porous material.

- -   1.  _Nitrogen adsorption_–_desorption_

The textural properties like the surface area, the pores nature and size of these activated carbon@metal oxide and their hydrogel beads were studied in order to better understand the adsorption properties of these materials. For this purpose, the nitrogen adsorption desorption isotherms at 77 K were carried out and represented in the [Fig. 3](#_bookmark21). It’s obvious that both activated carbon-based nanocomposites and chitosan-based hydrogel belong to the isotherm type IV according to the IUPAC classification which confirm mesoporous structure of these materials. This observation is also confirmed by their pore diameter generally varying in a range between 2 and 50 nm ([Table 1](#_bookmark22)). An evident decrease of the BET surface after the encapsulation of activated carbon@metal oxide in the chitosan matrix are observed which is mainly due to the pore blockage caused by the chitosan. Indeed, the chitosan is well known to be not highly porous and after encapsulating the activated carbon by this biopolymer, this encapsulation blocks smaller micropores

<2 nm, shifting the pore size distribution toward larger mesopores

(2–50 nm) \[[70](#_bookmark80)\]. This can reduce the overall BET surface area since micropores contribute significantly to surface area measurements. Moreover, the hydrogel structure of chitosan can act as a barrier, limiting the diffusion of gas molecules into the internal pores of

The AC@CaO, AC@Al2O3 and AC@CaO/Al2O3 showed a BET surface of 591.13, 686.32 and 648.51 m2/g while the CSAC@Ca, CSAC@Al and CSAC@ALCA showed a surface area of 264.28, 341.04 and 318.43 m2/g. This difference between the surface area of metal oxide-based materials can be explained by mainly the porosity and the behaviour of each metal oxide. For example, the composites with the highest pore volume and BET surface was the Al2O3\-based, this metal oxide is very stable, has naturally a high surface area and a mesoporous characteristic \[[72](#_bookmark82)\]. While the CaO has a lower porosity and a larger macropores, in addition to a tendency to agglomerate and sinter which reduce the available surface area of the resulting material leading to the lowest BET surface between the studied adsorbents \[[73](#_bookmark83)\]. For the CaO/Al2O3, the Al2O3 contributes high surface area and CaO introduces structural stability and additional adsorption sites. This synergy between calcium and aluminum prevents excessive sintering of CaO and conduce to a com-bination of micro-, meso-, and macropores leading to a broader pore distribution \[[74](#_bookmark84)\]. Another important parameter is responsible of these results which is the dispersion method. The sonication allowed the excellent dispersion of cationic metal into the biomass matrix and in a high amount, this excellent dispersion reduce the agglomeration which

generally is responsible of the surface area decrease. Moreover, since in the CaO/Al2O3 case, a competition occurs between the Ca+2 and Al+3, a lower quantity of metal oxide is generated during the calcination which

lead to a higher surface area of the resulting materials.

- 1.  _Adsorption study_
        1. _Effect of the pollutant initial concentration_

It’s well known that the initial concentration (C0) of a pollutant affect strongly the maximum adsorption capacity at equilibrium and have even an influence on the adsorption process \[[7](#_bookmark38)\]. so, in order to optimize the study of this effect, high concentrations of methylene blue and orange G were studied and the obtained results were represented in the [Fig. 4](#_bookmark23) (a, b). The Figures clearly show a rise in the amount of dye adsorbed in function of their initial concentration, which is natural given that a large quantity of an adsorbate tends to provide a strong inclusion, causing the dispersion of the dye toward the adsorbent and the retention of greater quantity of pollutants. Indeed, the amount of organic dyes adsorbed at equilibrium is generally higher when the initial concentration rise. However, this increase beyond a certain concentra-tion lead to a saturation of the active site of the material and the interruption of the adsorption process characterized by the constancy of Qe \[[7](#_bookmark38)\]. The results show that the adsorption capacity of pollutants by

these materials follows the following order: CST < CSAC@Ca < CSA-C@ALCA < CSAC@Al during the adsorption of methylene blue and follows the according order: CST < CSAC@Al < CSAC@ALCA <

CSAC@Ca during the adsorption of the orange G. Obviously, all adsor-bents showed good results and a clear superiority of the nanocomposites against both dyes compared to the chitosan beads. Several important factors affect strongly the adsorption order which are mainly the surface charge of the adsorbent and the pollutants, the specific surface area, porosity and the interactions between adsorbent/adsorbate. According to zeta potential analysis, the CSAC@Ca showed a more positive surface

charge which explain that this composite is more selective to anionic dyes molecules and the same thing for the CSAC@Al which is more favourable to cationic dye. For the superiority of the nanocomposite’s beads, this is mainly due to the presence of the activated carbon and the metal oxide which rise the specific surface area, the porosity and the available active site of the resulting composite.

- -   1.  _Effect of contact time_

The study of the contact time effect allows to evaluate the necessary time to reach equilibrium; it is the time from which the adsorbed con-centration does not evolve significantly \[[48](#_bookmark59)\]. For this purpose, the effect of contact time for both organic dyes were studied at C0 = 150 ppm, a

neutral pH and under ambient temperature. The obtained results shown

in the [Fig. 4](#_bookmark23) (c, d). confirm that around 50 % of the pollutants are adsorbed by the hydrogel’s beads in the first 30 min of contact time. Which is due to the large number of vacant active sites available during the adsorption process beginning \[[7](#_bookmark38),[48](#_bookmark59)\]. Then, the adsorbed quantity

continues to rise until _T_ \= 180 min which is the optimal contact time,

after that the adsorption processes become slow and the variation is not very high. This phenomenon is explained by the progressive consump-tion of the active sites until their saturation \[[14](#_bookmark42)\]. It’s clear that the or-ange G and methylene blue dyes continue to be adsorbed until a very advanced time which is due to the abundant adsorption sites such as the –NH2, –COOH, –OH available in the surface of the chitosan, the acti-vated carbon and the metal oxide and to the large porosity of the composite beads. The highest adsorption rate was observed from the CSAC@Al against the methylene blue and from CSAC@Ca against or-ange G, anyway the adsorption rate between the nanocomposites are closes but is much highest than the adsorption rate of the parent chitosan which confirm the superiority of these materials.

In order to understand the behaviour of the adsorbents and pollut-ants at each pH, the effect of pH on the quantity adsorbed was studied in a pH range of 2 to 10 and the obtained results are regrouped in the [Fig. 5](#_bookmark24) (a, b). The same adsorption order mentioned previously is observed in all the pH range with CSAC@Al and CSAC@Ca as the best adsorbent

against methylene blue and orange G respectively. In the MB case, the adsorption rate of all biosorbents was poor at pH = 2 and rise in function of pH rising which is due to the nature of this dye (cationic); indeed,

since the methylene blue structure has a cation that allow it to bind

- -   1.  _Effect of temperature_

The effect of temperature on the adsorption capacity of the chitosan and its nanocomposites beads was investigated by studying the adsorption process at different temperatures (28, 50 and 75 ◦C) and the

results obtained are regrouped in the [Fig. 5](#_bookmark24) (c, d). The first observation is

that the quantity of organic dyes adsorbed at equilibrium (Qe) increases when the temperature rise which confirm the endothermic nature of the MB and OG adsorption. This positive correlation can be explained by the fact that an activation of the biosorbents surface followed by a rise in the kinetic energy is generated by a high temperature in the reaction me-dium. This kinetic energy lead to a high mobility and collision between the organic dyes and the biosorbents in addition to a generation of several chemical bonds.

- -   1.  _Adsorption isotherm study_

The adsorption isotherms are an important part in any adsorption

study, it allows the determination of the maximum adsorption capacity (Qmax) of the materials used and allows us to determinate the nature of adsorption process \[[48](#_bookmark59),[75](#_bookmark85)\]. Many theoretical models exist to describe the adsorption isotherms but, in our study, the Langmuir and Freundlich isotherm models considered as the simplest, efficient and popular were chosen to describe the adsorption behaviour of organic dyes onto the chitosan-based composites since they best fit with the experimental data and provide meaningful insights into the adsorption mechanism. The Langmuir isotherm was applied, as it assumes monolayer adsorption on a homogeneous surface with a finite number of identical binding sites, and the high correlation coefficient (R2) obtained suggests that a sig-nificant portion of the adsorption follows this mechanism. Additionally, the Langmuir maximum adsorption capacity (Qmax) allows for a quan-titative comparison of adsorbent efficiency. Alongside this, the Freundlich isotherm was evaluated due to its consideration of surface heterogeneity and multilayer adsorption, which is relevant for complex adsorbents, where adsorption energies may vary across the surface.

Furthermore, the Freundlich exponent (n) provides insight into adsorption favourability, with _n_ \> 1 indicating a favourable adsorption process \[[14](#_bookmark42),[26](#_bookmark48)\]. For this reason, the adsorption capacity of the chitosan-

based beads against the methylene blue and orange G using the Lang-muir and Freundlich models is represented in the [Fig. 6](#_bookmark25), and summa-rized in [Table 2](#_bookmark26). By examining the figure results and the correlation coefficients (R2), it’s obvious that both organic dyes follow the Langmuir isotherm with an R2 near to 1 which confirms that the adsorption of MB and OG dyes is a uniform and monolayer adsorption. By comparing the

maximum adsorption capacity Qmax, the CSAC@Al showed the best adsorption capacity of MB with a Qmax = 134.589 mg/g, whereas for the OG adsorption CSAC@Ca was the best with Qmax = 323.625 mg/g. The adsorption rate of orange G was higher than methylene blue for all

biosorbent including the chitosan beads. Numerous factors, including the pollutant’s and adsorbent’s surface charges, surface area, pore size, and the various ways the nanocomposite and the pollutant interact, contribute to this selectivity; Indeed, it has been observed from the zeta potential analysis that all materials showed a positive surface charge at all the pH range which make them directly selective to the anionic dye instead of the cationic. Finally, a comparison between our hydrogel and other sorbents reported in the literature was carried out to evaluate their performance in the adsorption process (see [Table 3](#_bookmark27)). From the table, these biocompatible and inexpensive chitosan-based hydrogels showed a better adsorption capacity against both the methylene blue and orange G than several well-known adsorbents with high porosity found in the literature, even regarding the complexity and the price of some of these reported adsorbents which certifies the effectiveness of our hydrogels beads and highlight the importance of the encapsulation by carbohy-drate polymers in eliminating contaminants.

- -   1.  _Adsorption kinetics_

The kinetic study is thought to be the most effective method of characterizing the adsorption behaviour. It is crucial to comprehend the basic mechanisms and interactions between the pollutant/adsorbent and to anticipate them through time. So, the pseudo-first order and pseudo-second order kinetic models were modeled to determine which model fit better with the experimental data. The results are summarized in [Table 1](#_bookmark22).S (see the supplementary data) and displayed in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark28). Ac-cording to the table, the regression coefficient R2 were higher where the pseudo-second order model is used with values near to 1 for all materials and both dyes as opposed to the pseudo-first model which showed a R2 in the range (0.760 to 0.835). Furthermore, the pseudo-second order model’s adsorption capacity Qe2 were closer to the experimental Qe unlike those of the pseudo-first one which confirm that the adsorption of methylene blue and orange G follow the pseudo-second-order model in the case of all hydrogel’s beads meaning that this adsorption process is more a chemisorption.

- -   1.  _Thermodynamic analysis_

In adsorption studies, thermodynamic parameters—specifically the enthalpy variation (ΔH◦), entropy variation (ΔS◦), and Gibbs free en-ergy variation (ΔG◦)—are critical for elucidating process mechanisms and quantifying the temperature dependence of pollutant adsorption. To

investigate this, the thermodynamic behaviour of methylene blue and orange G adsorption was analysed at three temperatures (301, 323, and 348 K). The obtained results are regrouped in [Table. 2](#_bookmark26)S and represented

as linear Van’t Hoff plots of ln KL vs 1/T in [Fig. 8](#_bookmark29). For MB adsorption, the positive ΔH◦ values (ΔH◦ = 18.856–19.371 J/mol for CSAC@Al, CSA-C@ALCA, and CSAC@Ca). Similarly, OG adsorption exhibited positive ΔH◦ values (10.602–19.413 J/mol), with CSAC@Ca showing the highest

ΔH◦ (19.413 J/mol). These enthalpies confirm the endothermic

character of the adsorption is indicated by the study of the dye adsorption data, characterized by a positive ΔH◦ engendered by heat gain during successive temperature rises. The endothermicity suggests

also that the energy generated from the temperature rise, promote stronger interactions (electrostatic interaction, ion exchange and π–π stacking) between the adsorbent’s functional groups (–NH2, –COOH, –OH, Ca2+, Al3+) and dye molecules \[[84](#_bookmark94)\]. On the other hand, the pos-

itive ΔS◦ suggest that the adsorption between dyes molecules and the

biosorbents occurs randomly at the solid-liquid interface and indicate increased system disorder during adsorption \[[7](#_bookmark38),[85](#_bookmark95)\]. The disorder in-crease is highly due to solvated water molecules moving away from the

adsorbent’s pores/surface and replaced by dye molecules which occupy binding spots \[[7](#_bookmark38),[85](#_bookmark95)\]. The correlation between endothermic ΔH◦ and positive ΔS◦ strongly supports a chemisorption mechanism rather than physisorption (e.g. hydrogen bonding and van der Waals interactions).

Moreover, the nature of the adsorption process was found to be

- -   1.  _Adsorption mechanism_

The valuable results obtained from different adsorption parameters and the characterization information’s allows to suggest a plausible mechanism of the adsorption by these chitosan-based composites ([Scheme 2](#_bookmark30)). From all these previous results, the chemisorption appears to be the most predominant type and the adsorption is an endothermic, uniform and monolayer adsorption. Several interactions types are involved in the methylene blue and orange G adsorption. Indeed, the hydrogen bonding, Van Der Waals interactions, pore fitting due to the presence of the activated carbon, π–π interactions between the dye’s aromatic rings with the aromatic ring of activated carbon by a direct π–π stacking, n–π interactions between the –NH2, –COOH, –OH groups, metal oxide oxygen lone pair at the surface of the beads and the π–system of the organic dyes are noticed; Then due to the presence of metal oxide, ion exchange is also visible since the adsorbent provide

**Scheme 2.** Schematic illustration of the adsorption mechanism of methylene blue and orange G by chitosan-based composite beads.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)Ca2+ and Al3+ exchange them with organic dyes ions. However, the electrostatic interactions especially as acid-base ionic bonding are the most predominant \[[86–88](#_bookmark96)\]. To classify them properly from strongest to

the weakest the interaction follows the following order: the electrostatic interactions > π–π stacking > ion exchange > hydrogen bonding/VDW interactions. According to the Zeta potential analysis and the effect of

pH. The chitosan and its nanocomposites beads show a positive surface charge at all pH range, at acidic condition a high concentration of the H3O+ is generated leading to the protonation of the –NH2 groups into

–NH+ thus provoking the formation of ionic acid-base bond with the

3

–SO— group of the orange G and attractive interaction with this dye, and cause repulsive interaction with the methylene blue. From neutral to

3

basic pH, the concentration of the OH— ions increase in the solution

causing the partial deprotonation of some –NH2, –COOH, –OH groups into –NH—, –COO—, –O respectively which lead to the generation of attractive and ionic interaction between these deprotonated groups and

the methylene blue and physical interaction between the unprotonated groups and the anionic dye “OG” due to the positive surface charge of these biosorbents \[[53](#_bookmark63)\]. The porosity of these chitosan-based adsorbent plays also a key role in their adsorption performance. The variation in the mesopores size distribution and surface area among the materials facilitates the diffusion of dye molecules into the internal surface of the adsorbents and the accessibility of active sites, enhancing overall dye retention. Indeed, this better accessibility enables stronger physical and chemical interactions especially after the protonation of the active functional groups. Thus, the porosity and surface charge contribute directly to the adsorption capacity by optimizing dye transport, contact time, and molecular interaction within the adsorbent structure. The synergistic effect of the combination of activated carbon, metal oxide and the biopolymer must also be highlighted since it can strongly improve the adsorption capacity of the obtained nanocomposites beads, by observing the adsorption capacity of the chitosan beads compared to its composites the efficiency is much higher. The encapsulation of the activated carbon/metal oxide into the chitosan provided more active adsorption sites and an additional surface area, and the presence of the biopolymer in these composites allowed the separation, recovery and the reuse of these biosorbents.

To summarize all adsorption mechanisms, electrostatic interactions

are the strongest and most dominant adsorption mechanism in this study. MB+ as a cationic dye, interacts with negatively charged surface groups such as –NH—, –COO—, –O available in chitosan and activated

carbon, while in case of anionic dye the OG— binds to positively charged sites, including protonated –NH+ groups and metal cations such as Ca2+ and Al3+. π–π stacking also plays a significant role, particularly with activated carbon, whose aromatic rings interact with the π-electron

3

system of both MB and OG dyes. Although π–π stacking is a phys-isorption mechanism and generally weaker than electrostatic attraction,

it remains an important mechanism of adsorption. Additionally, ion exchange provides a moderate contribution, as exchangeable Ca2+ and Al3+ ions from the metal oxides can be replaced by MB+ in a cationic exchange process or bind OG— in an anionic exchange mechanism which explains the enhanced adsorption capacity of metal oxide-containing

composites. In case of the CSAC@ALCA, the effect is strongest due to its dual ion exchange capability but due to the lower porosity, amor-phous phase and lower metal content, its efficiency is intermediate be-tween the CSAC@Al and CSAC@Ca. Finally, hydrogen bonding and VDW interactions, although the most weak compared the other mech-anisms, it helps to strongly stabilizes adsorption. Hydrogen bonds generated between –NH2, –COOH, –OH groups on chitosan/activated

carbon and functional groups on the dye molecules, such as –SO— in OG

3

and amine groups in MB.

- -   1.  _Adsorbents reusability_

The reusability of these chitosan-based nanocomposites was studied by carrying out the adsorption of methylene blue and orange G during 5 continuous cycles without any treatment and the obtained results were represented in the [Fig. 9](#_bookmark31). Due to their beads form and their properties observed from FTIR, SEM and zeta potential analysis such as the large surface area, high porosity and abundant functional groups, these ma-terials can easy be separated, recovered and reused several times as observed from the figure. The reusability effectiveness of the chitosan-based nanocomposite was very clear contrary to the chitosan beads “CST” which is mainly due to the lack of porosity and the reduced sur-face area compared to its nanocomposite. Indeed, the encapsulation of activated carbon and metal oxide provided more surface specific and more active site for adsorption in addition to several interaction with the pollutants. The lack of these parameters in the case of parent chitosan lead to a very quick saturation of the adsorption and a very low quantity adsorbed during the two last cycles. It can also be observed that in the case of G orange, the adsorbed amount is significantly reduced after the first use because of the occupation of a large number of adsorption sites due to the affinity between these hydrogels and the anionic dye, while for methylene blue, the amount adsorbed decreases slowly due to the repulsive interaction between the positively charged surface of the chitosan-based materials and the cationic dye, leading to gradual adsorption and a less important surface/pores occupation over the cy-cles. This phenomenon is known as surface fouling which means that over multiple cycles, residual dye molecules may remain strongly bound to active sites, reducing available adsorption sites and a pore blockage. Finally, the percentages of the adsorbed quantity decrease in the case of methylene blue were between 27 % to 32 % and between 33 % to 36 % in the case of orange G which confirm the effectiveness of these bio-sorbents even after several cycles of adsorption.

- -   1.  _Effect of the metal oxide on the adsorption process_

In order to show the real effect of the presence of metal oxide nanoparticles, adsorption tests of both cationic and anionic dye adsorption were carried out, and a comparison between metal oxide-based composites and chitosan@activated carbon composite (CSAC) was performed. Fig. 1S regroups the obtained results (See the supple-mentary data). The results show that the metal-oxide-free adsorbent (CSAC) showed reduced adsorption capacity against both cationic and anionic dyes compared to the metal oxide-based adsorbents, which emphasises the role of CaO and Al2O3 in providing additional active sites and improving adsorption efficiency. Moreover, the presence of metal oxide provides more interactions with organic dyes compared to CSAC such as the ion exchange and possible chelation; in addition to

amplification of existing interaction, such as the electrostatic interaction which enables a higher adsorption capacity. The same conclusion was proved by the previous studies of A. Iles et al. and Zhi-Feng Yang et al., where a similar comparison between adsorbents with and without metal oxide was carried out and the metal oxide’s crucial role was highlighted \[[26](#_bookmark48),[89](#_bookmark97)\].

# Conclusion

The hydrogel composite beads based on activated carbon@metal oxide (M: CaO, Al2O3, CaO/Al2O3) from the calcination of metallic cation dispersed on olive stones biomass and encapsulated by chitosan as a cross-linking matrix. These biocomposites were characterized by different techniques such as SEM (inside and outside the bead), TGA, Zeta potential, XRD and FTIR in order to investigate their structural, thermal and morphological properties. From the FTIR and XRD analyses, the desired structure of the activated carbon@metal oxide-based nano-composites and chitosan/ activated carbon@metal oxide are well confirmed. The SEM confirmed the porous structure of the hydrogels beads due to the presence of the activated carbon and the well dispersed metal oxide particles due to the ultrasonic treatments use which allowed

a very good dispersion of Cu+2, Al+3 and/or Ca+2/Al+3 in the olive stone

biomass before calcination. Zeta potential shows that all chitosan-based composites have a positive surface charge in all pH range even at very acidic pH confirming thus the encapsulation in the chitosan which is a biopolymer well known for its very positive surface charge. The adsorption experimental data confirmed that the organic dyes adsorp-tion follows the Langmuir isotherm which means that the dyes are adsorbed in a uniform monolayer adsorption. With a correlation coef-ficient close to 1, the kinetic study demonstrates that the pseudo-second order model describes better the organic dyes adsorption. The thermo-dynamic study confirmed that the adsorption of MB and OG by these hydrogel beads is endothermic, random and spontaneous reaction, and proved also the chemisorption nature of the adsorption. The adsorption analysis revealed a variety of chemical and physical interactions; the hydrogen bonding, Van Der Waals interactions, pore fitting due to the presence of the activated carbon, π–π interactions between the dye’s aromatic rings with the aromatic ring of activated carbon by a direct π–π stacking, n–π interactions between the –NH2, –COOH, –OH groups, metal oxide oxygen lone pair at the surface of the beads and the π–system of the organic dyes are noticed; Then due to the presence of metal oxide, ion exchange is also visible since the adsorbent provide

Ca2+ and Al3+ exchange them with organic dyes ions. However, the electrostatic interactions especially as acid-base ionic bonding are the

most predominant.

These carbohydrate-based composites have confirmed their effi-ciency as an excellent biosorbent due to their various interactions with the dyes, the abundance of active adsorption sites, the large surface area; the high porosity conferred by the activated carbon and the dispersion of the presence of metal oxide which increase the adsorption capacity significantly. The ability of these chitosan-based adsorbents to simul-taneously capture both cationic and anionic pollutants is mainly attributed to the presence of both positively and negatively charged

functional sites within the composite structure. Chitosan, with its pro-tonated amine groups (–NH+) at acidic pH, provides sites for anionic dye adsorption, while deprotonated hydroxyl (–OH) and carboxyl (–COO—)

3

groups facilitate cationic dye adsorption. Moreover, the dispersion of CaO and Al2O3 introduces metal cation sites (Ca2+, Al3+), which

enhance electrostatic interactions and ion exchange processes which strengthening the dye adsorption capability. The beads shape and size are also a very important parameters since it allow the use, the sepa-ration and the reuse of the biosorbents during several cycle offering a potential large-scale environmental application due to their reusability, long-term stability, and affordability under real-world conditions.
